column1: 001|A thin line crosses an ancient animal bone. At first glance, it looks like the beginning of a hunting story. Look closer. Someone else may have written it.|Extreme macro slider across one shallow groove on a clean adult antelope limb-bone teaching replica resting on a dark modern laboratory tray; warm raking light reveals texture.

002|Imagine the scene we are tempted to build: a hunter, a stone blade, a successful meal. Yet the bone preserves a mark, not the scene we imagined.|A mature researcher aged 45 holds a smooth unmodified stone flake beside, without contacting, a clean animal bone replica; slow medium side dolly in a contemporary laboratory.

003|A tooth could leave a line. So could a stone pushed through gritty ground. Even the beautiful shape of a scratch can have more than one origin.|A transparent teaching model shows three separate unlabelled blunt and sharp contact shapes hovering above three cream synthetic bone strips; gentle overhead descent, no contact transformation.

004|The dangerous step is small: we turn evidence of damage into evidence of a meal, then turn that meal into a confident claim about a hunt.|Low lateral track past three separate unlabelled display trays containing a scratched animal bone cast, a plain stone flake, and a blank wooden spear replica; modern teaching exhibit.

005|But who touched the bone? Who arrived first? And who, if anyone, killed the animal? Those are three different questions, and they demand different kinds of evidence.|A clean animal bone cast rotates slowly on a plain dark manual turntable, viewed through a large magnifying lens; close side push, modern research bench.

006|Our investigation begins with the smallest question: what physically made this mark? The answer could move an entire prehistoric story in a different direction.|Microscope objective descends slowly toward a clean synthetic bone coupon held in a modern specimen cradle; locked close camera with a controlled focus pull.

007|We will meet heavy jaws, pointed teeth, moving sediment, and a surprisingly complicated claw. We will also discover why a genuine tool mark cannot tell us everything.|An adult spotted hyena stands calmly at the edge of dry grass in a generic African landscape, mouth closed, no prey; long-lens slow lateral slide from a safe distant viewpoint.

008|There is a word for the journey from a living animal to an excavated bone: taphonomy. It studies the changes that happened along the way.|Slow aerial glide above a generic dry river terrace with exposed sediment layers and sparse vegetation; no people, no bones, no survey markings.

009|That journey may involve many visitors across many years. A fossil can preserve several encounters, while hiding the moments we would most like to see.|A clean adult-animal bone replica lies partly embedded in a transparent layered sediment teaching box; low macro slide across distinct sand and silt layers, modern demonstration.

010|The mystery is not whether ancient people hunted. It is whether the particular evidence in front of us supports the particular story we want to tell.|Wide slow dolly into a contemporary archaeology laboratory where two clearly mature researchers examine separate trays; screens turned away, no readable labels or figures.
011|So keep that first narrow groove in mind. Before we call it a hunter's signature, we must let the other possible authors enter the room.|REUSE:001

012|Start with the surface, not the story. A bone has hard outer tissue, curved edges, dense shafts, and joint ends. These respond differently to contact.|A mature anatomist slowly turns a clean adult deer limb-bone replica to reveal shaft and enlarged joint end; close overhead orbit in a modern teaching laboratory.

013|A tooth pressed into a surface may leave a pit. A tooth dragged across it may leave a score. Stronger contact can penetrate or remove material.|Slow macro orbit around three separate cream synthetic bone coupons with a round depression, a long groove, and a deeper hole; all clearly modern teaching samples.

014|These names describe forms we can observe. They do not, by themselves, identify a species, a meal, or the order in which events took place.|A mature researcher places three small blank neutral tokens beside three artificial marked coupons without sorting them; static overhead view with a gradual focus pull.

015|Researchers examine depth, width, shape, internal texture, and the surrounding surface. They also ask where a mark sits on the whole bone, and what accompanies it.|A modern optical surface microscope scans along an animal-bone cast on a motorised stage; slow close lateral camera movement, display facing away.

016|A narrow groove may look different when the light changes. A shadow can make one wall appear deeper, while a photograph can conceal its actual cross section.|The same synthetic groove remains still while a single raking laboratory lamp moves gently from left to right; fixed macro view, physically consistent shadows.

017|This is why one dramatic close-up is a beginning, not a verdict. We need observations that other people can inspect, compare, and challenge independently.|Two mature laboratory researchers inspect matching casts at adjacent desks through separate magnifiers; medium lateral dolly, no visible writing or screen content.

018|Consider a sharp stone edge and a rough tooth surface. Both can contact bone. Their traces can overlap in appearance without coming from the same action.|Macro push toward a plain stone flake and a clearly resin-cast adult carnivore tooth arranged separately beside a smooth synthetic bone coupon; no tissue.

019|A familiar rule says a V-shaped groove means cutting, while a rounded groove means chewing. It is a useful starting intuition, not a universal identification key.|Two large teaching blocks show contrasting angular and rounded channel cross sections, cream resin on a charcoal table; slow low orbit, no letters or measurement markings.

020|Real marks vary with the contacting surface, movement, pressure, and condition of the bone. A single outline cannot carry the weight of an entire reconstruction.|A mature technician adjusts an unlabelled mechanical contact-testing rig above an artificial bone strip; medium side tracking, no active breaking or biological material.

021|And there is an even simpler problem. We sometimes name a mark after the animal we expected to find, then mistake that expectation for an observation.|A closed field notebook without lettering sits beside a clean bone cast and a magnifier; slow close dolly past the objects, contemporary research bench.

022|The first discipline of this investigation is therefore restraint: describe what is visible before deciding what caused it. Now let us bring in the teeth.|Slow macro track toward a resin cast of an adult hyena jaw in a modern museum drawer; no skull or human material, no labels.

023|Carnivores do not all treat food in the same way. Different teeth, feeding actions, and opportunities can leave different patterns of damage on animal remains.|Two mature adult carnivores, a spotted hyena and a lion, appear in separate distant natural habitat zones divided by foreground vegetation; slow wide lateral glide, no encounter or feeding.

024|A hyena's powerful jaws make it an obvious suspect when bones are heavily altered. But recognising a plausible agent is different from identifying every mark it produced.|An adult spotted hyena walks calmly across a rocky open landscape in early morning; low long-lens tracking, mouth closed, no prey, no remains.

025|On comparative specimens, researchers may find pits, punctures, scores, and damaged edges together. The combination can be more informative than the most spectacular individual scar.|Close overhead descent toward several clean adult-animal bone teaching casts with different simulated surface modifications arranged in separate neutral trays; modern lab.

026|Location matters. Marks around a joint and marks on a shaft need to be considered within anatomy and feeding behaviour, rather than counted as identical events.|A gloved mature hand points without touching to a replica joint end, then rests beside the shaft; close side slide, contemporary anatomy teaching bench.

027|A very deep mark is not automatically the earliest mark. A shallow mark is not automatically human. The dramatic appearance of damage does not establish its history.|Macro focus pull between a shallow linear groove and a deep rounded depression on two separate synthetic coupons; cool modern laboratory lighting.

028|Nor should every broken bone be assigned to a particular predator. Breakage can come from several processes, and missing pieces may remove the most useful comparisons.|A mature conservator gently aligns two already separated clean resin animal-bone fragments on soft foam without forcing a join; slow overhead orbit.

029|The living animal helps us understand what is possible. A reference collection helps us compare the traces. Neither allows us to invent an ancient encounter we never observed.|Wide push down a modern museum reference room aisle with closed plain drawers; a mature researcher carries a small tray, no readable records.

030|That distinction matters because familiar predators draw our attention. A lion or hyena fits an easy story. Another powerful bone-marking animal may be waiting beside the water.|Slow low glide along a generic warm African riverbank, reeds moving in a breeze, adult crocodile partly visible far away; no other animals, no attack.

031|Its teeth can do something especially troublesome for anyone hoping to identify a stone blade from a few narrow marks. The next suspect is a crocodile.|An adult Nile crocodile rests calmly on a sandbank with mouth closed; controlled long-lens push toward the textured snout from a visibly distant wildlife perspective.

032|A mouth does not need a stone tool to make a sharp-looking trace. We need to study how contact occurred, not simply what object a groove resembles.|Macro orbit around a resin crocodile tooth cast with a subtle natural-looking ridge, placed beside a synthetic scratched bone coupon; modern laboratory, no real jaw movement.
033|Keep our original groove in view. Once several agents can make something similar, the investigation must grow beyond that one line into patterns, experiments, and context.|REUSE:001

034|In research published in two thousand six, Jackson Njau and Robert Blumenschine described feeding traces produced by Nile crocodiles, using observations and comparative bone collections.|A mature contemporary researcher opens a plain reference drawer containing clean resin animal-bone casts and crocodile tooth casts in separate recesses; medium side dolly.

035|The study helped establish that crocodiles could leave distinctive combinations of tooth marks and other damage. Some traces deserved attention in ancient river and lake settings.|Slow aerial movement above an anonymous East African lake margin with reed beds and exposed sediment terraces; no settlement reconstruction or map graphics.

036|This did not mean every fossil beside water was a crocodile meal. It meant an important alternative could no longer be left outside the comparison.|A mature geologist examines a dry sediment outcrop well away from the river, holding a closed specimen tray; wide lateral tracking in a generic field setting.

037|Then a two thousand seventeen study by Yonatan Sahle and colleagues revisited ancient Ethiopian material in the light of crocodile feeding damage and competing explanations.|Two mature researchers compare two cream animal-bone casts beneath magnifiers at a contemporary laboratory table; slow medium orbit, no manuscript text.

038|Their warning was methodological: different processes can make similar-looking products. Archaeologists call this equifinality. It is the reason a convincing resemblance may still be misleading.|Three differently shaped resin contact tools sit behind three similar artificial groove specimens, arranged on separate dark blocks; slow overhead slide, no diagram labels.

039|Picture three paths reaching the same doorway. The doorway alone does not tell you which path was taken. A groove can pose a similar problem.|A clearly schematic physical landscape model shows three shallow branching tracks approaching one neutral depression; gentle overhead descent, no people, buildings, lettering or map claims.

040|Crocodile comparisons do not erase genuine evidence of stone-tool use. They make our tests more demanding, especially when the proposed event rests on very few marks.|Close side track past a stone flake, resin crocodile tooth, and three separate synthetic coupons, with objects remaining physically distinct; contemporary research bench.

041|This is where a documentary can become too confident. A reconstructed bite looks persuasive on screen, but the animation is an illustration, not an independent observation.|A mature science filmmaker slowly moves a small camera on a slider beside an unlabelled synthetic groove teaching model; medium view in a modern studio.

042|Our own images will keep the alternatives separate. The evidence must do the deciding. A vivid scene cannot supply the missing information that the bone does not contain.|A mature researcher closes a blank drawer containing illustrative resin casts while an actual microscope remains in focus nearby; slow focus pull across the lab bench.

043|And teeth are not the only rivals to a sharp cutting edge. We now need a suspect with no jaws, no intention, and no appetite at all.|Low slow dolly across a dry sandy surface with small angular stones and a partly visible clean synthetic bone coupon; controlled modern outdoor experiment.

044|Watch what happens when bone, grit, and movement meet. A scratch can be made by the ground, even when no one intended to cut anything.|Macro side tracking of a clean artificial bone coupon moving slowly across coarse sand under an unlabelled laboratory rig; no human or animal feet.

045|Imagine a bone resting among sharp grains. Pressure brings them together. Movement lets a grain travel across the surface, leaving damage that may resemble deliberate cutting.|A large transparent tabletop model holds a cream synthetic bone strip above a bed of angular resin grains; slow close orbit, clearly an educational model.

046|Experiments on trampling have explored this problem for decades. Studies in the nineteen eighties showed why researchers needed to compare accidental abrasion with traces from processing animals.|Mature gloved hands arrange paired artificial samples from separate experimental trays on a modern bench; slow overhead descent, no actual cutting, flesh or text.

047|We should not reduce that work to another shortcut: many random scratches means trampling, one neat scratch means a tool. Nature does not promise such tidy categories.|Macro lateral slide across several separate teaching coupons bearing varied simulated scratches, some isolated and some clustered; balanced neutral laboratory light.

048|The relevant comparison includes the substrate, the motion, the condition of the surface, and the range of results. An experiment becomes useful when those conditions are documented.|A modern technician adjusts a clear sand-box testing apparatus with interchangeable rounded and angular grains in separate dishes; medium side dolly, controls unmarked.

049|A microscopic study examined variation within trampling marks, including scratches and grazes. Even one broad process can produce several kinds of damage, not a single signature.|Close orbit around two clearly artificial teaching blocks, one with a fine groove and one with a broad shallow abraded patch; modern optical lab.

050|This makes an important difference to our reasoning. A fossil does not fail to be human-made merely because an alternative exists. We must compare how well alternatives fit.|A mature researcher moves two separate resin comparison coupons beside one central specimen cast, leaving space between them; slow overhead track, no verdict symbols.

051|Suppose an ancient surface retains a deep line but has lost its finest texture. The missing detail may be exactly what would help us distinguish competing causes.|Extreme macro focus pull along a synthetic groove whose far end is deliberately smoothed in a modern teaching cast; texture visible, no invented measurements.

052|An absence of tiny scratches can then become ambiguous. Were they never made, or did later processes remove the part of the surface that once carried them?|A mature conservator tilts an artificial worn coupon beneath one fixed lamp, revealing smooth and textured zones; close lateral glide, no treatment applied.

053|The same caution applies to a specimen collected from the ground surface. Finding it is valuable; knowing precisely where it originated is a separate geological question.|An adult field researcher aged 50 stands beside a generic eroding outcrop and examines an empty neutral specimen container; wide slow side dolly, no staged fossil discovery.

054|Sediment is therefore not just the material we brush away to find the interesting object. It can be part of the explanation for the object itself.|A mature geologist lifts a small transparent sample box containing separate coarse sand and fine silt layers; macro push, no bone extraction or readable labels.
055|Return to that moving grain. It has no intention to deceive us. The error begins when we allow a familiar-looking line to settle the question too soon.|REUSE:044

056|Now consider the claw. Its shape seems to promise a dramatic answer, especially when several parallel scratches appear. But resemblance still needs a tested physical explanation.|An adult tiger walks calmly through a quiet woodland enclosure with natural vegetation, no visitors or other animals; distant long-lens lateral tracking, no attack or scratching.

057|A study published in two thousand thirteen documented bone damage associated with striking claws during captive tiger enrichment. It widened the possibilities researchers needed to consider.|A modern teaching display holds a resin adult tiger paw cast beside an untouched synthetic bone strip, physically separated; slow medium orbit, no live action.

058|That finding does not turn every parallel scratch into a tiger trace. It shows why a plausible mechanism must be checked against observations, rather than assumed impossible.|Macro side slide along three separate artificial scratched coupons beside a closed neutral storage box; no animal imagery, no identification labels.

059|The same lesson holds for rodents. Gnawing can create repeated grooves, yet even their dimensions may support a size range more readily than a precise species name.|An adult gray squirrel moves calmly along a fallen branch in a modern woodland, no bone or food in its mouth; steady close wildlife tracking.

060|A study of rodent and rabbit gnawing found that identifying a particular species from damage alone was often difficult. The most responsible answer could remain broader.|A mature comparative anatomist sets resin incisor casts of different adult-animal sizes into separate plain holders; slow overhead descent, no skulls or writing.

061|An investigator gains nothing by naming an animal more precisely than the evidence allows. Uncertainty about the culprit can be an accurate result, not an unfinished thought.|An adult researcher places a clean animal-bone cast into an individual foam recess and closes the plain tray lid; medium close dolly, calm deliberate action.

062|Other changes have no feeding animal behind them. Roots, weathering, abrasion, and chemical conditions can modify a surface during the long interval before its recovery.|Slow macro glide beside branching plant roots in a transparent soil teaching box, with a separate clean animal-bone replica visible behind the clear wall.

063|Weathering studies remind us that preservation has a history of its own. Cracking and surface loss change what remains available for later examination and comparison.|Macro orbit around two clearly synthetic teaching casts of adult-animal bone, one smooth and one showing simulated dry surface cracking; no breaking action.

064|We cannot read those changes as a universal clock. Conditions differ between places, and an exposed bone does not experience the same environment as a buried one.|A clear physical teaching model shows two identical animal-bone replicas in separate settings, one above dry sand and one beneath layered sediment; slow overhead slide.

065|By now our original suspect list has become much longer. This should make us more careful, not helpless. Multiple causes require better comparisons, not an abandonment of evidence.|A mature scientist slowly opens a plain cabinet of neatly separated synthetic reference samples; wide gentle push, no clutter, labels or computer display.
066|We are finally ready to bring the stone edge back. Its case must be made positively, through converging evidence, rather than by ignoring every competing explanation.|REUSE:018

067|When a tool contacts bone during processing, it can leave surface damage. Researchers examine its morphology together with anatomical position and the broader pattern of modification.|Close overhead tracking across a clean adult deer limb-bone cast resting next to a plain stone flake on a modern comparative anatomy table; objects remain separate.

068|A mark near a place where tissue attaches may carry different implications from a stray line on another surface. Anatomy helps turn appearance into a testable question.|A mature anatomist points with a soft blunt probe to a natural ridge on a clean adult-animal bone replica; close side push, no tissue or cutting.

069|Several observations become stronger when they agree. But agreement is not simply the number of photographs showing the same scratch. We need different kinds of relevant information.|Three contemporary researchers examine a specimen cast, sediment sample, and plain stone flake at separate stations; slow medium lateral dolly, all clearly mature.

070|For example, the shape of a mark, its position, and associated damage may be compared with reference material. The geological setting asks a different, equally necessary question.|A modern teaching table holds a bone cast, transparent sediment block and separate stone sample in a clean triangular arrangement; controlled overhead orbit, no markings.

071|A stone found nearby does not automatically explain a bone's history. The connection must be supported by the way materials were deposited, preserved, and recovered together.|Wide slow lateral track past a clearly modern excavation practice box containing separately embedded stone and animal-bone replicas at visibly different depths; no authentic site claim.

072|Percussion adds another layer. Striking a bone with a stone can leave impact-related features as well as breakage. These need comparison with damage from other agents.|A mature technician adjusts a stationary rounded stone and anvil above a synthetic bone strip in a controlled laboratory rig; close side dolly, no strike or break.

073|Research published in nineteen eighty-eight described percussion marks as useful evidence when examined with associated impact notches and microscopic characteristics. One isolated pit could still be misleading.|Macro focus pull across a resin teaching replica with a simulated impact notch beside a separate rounded depression sample; modern lab, no tissue or numbers.

074|It is the relationship among features that matters. A break, a pit, and a groove do not become three independent confirmations merely because we list them separately.|A gloved mature hand turns one clean resin animal-bone fragment showing three artificial teaching features; slow close orbit, realistic surface and no annotations.

075|The investigator must ask whether a single process could have produced several of them together. Otherwise, one event can be counted repeatedly as if it were several witnesses.|A physical demonstration places three unlabelled casts of different views of the same synthetic fragment beside one original teaching model; slow overhead descent.

076|All of this may sound cautious. Yet the stakes explain why it matters: a few marks can become evidence for when our ancestors first used tools on animals.|Slow aerial glide over an anonymous dry East African badlands landscape with layered cliffs; no people, animals, chronology graphics or authenticated map layout.

077|That possibility made two fossil specimens from Ethiopia famous. Their debate shows what happens when a tiny surface carries an exceptionally large claim about the past.|A mature curator places two clean generic adult-animal bone casts in separate foam trays beneath a soft laboratory lamp; close side tracking, explicitly illustrative replicas.

078|In two thousand ten, researchers reported marks on two animal bones from Dikika, Ethiopia, interpreting them as evidence of stone-tool-assisted processing before three point three nine million years ago.|Wide slow glide along a generic Ethiopian Afar dry landscape with pale sediment exposures, distant hills and sparse shrubs; no people, specimens, dates or site-plan claims.

079|The claim was striking because it placed that behaviour deep in the Pliocene. But the specimens did not arrive with a preserved explanation of what made each mark.|A mature researcher studies an anonymous animal-bone teaching cast through a large magnifier in a contemporary laboratory; slow focus pull from the whole cast to its surface.

080|Critics questioned whether the marks and their context securely excluded trampling and related processes. Their challenge concerned the connection between visible damage and the event being inferred.|Slow overhead slide across a clean animal-bone cast, coarse sediment dish and separate synthetic trampling coupon; modern comparative experiment, no actual fossils.

081|The original researchers defended their interpretation. The discussion involved details of surfaces, comparisons, and geological context, rather than a simple choice between liking or disliking an exciting discovery.|Two mature researchers independently inspect separate casts at a shared laboratory bench, expressions thoughtful and neutral; medium lateral dolly, no argument or printed papers.

082|In two thousand fifteen, a broader study of Dikika fossils argued that trampling was not the most economical explanation for the disputed specimens. More comparative context changed the discussion.|Wide overhead descent toward many clean generic adult-animal bone replicas arranged in separate foam compartments in a modern reference room; no exact dataset or specimen count claimed.

083|This is a useful moment to pause. A scientific disagreement can generate new observations and better comparisons. It should not be edited into a tale of heroes exposing villains.|A mature lab researcher hands a plain closed specimen box to another mature colleague; smooth medium side track, calm cooperative contemporary setting.

084|Nor should a documentary announce that the dispute proves every ancient cut mark is doubtful. Evidence must be assessed at the level of the particular specimen and assemblage.|Slow macro orbit around one generic synthetic marked animal-bone coupon isolated on a dark research bench; soft background reference trays, no lettering.

085|The Dikika discussion is valuable because it exposes the steps between an observation and a historical conclusion. Each step can be examined, and sometimes challenged, separately.|A clean physical teaching arrangement shows three separate small workstations: magnifier, reference casts and sediment box; one continuous slow lateral dolly, no arrows or labels.

086|An age estimate, a surface interpretation, and an argument about behaviour answer different questions. Confidence in one does not automatically make the others equally secure.|Close overhead orbit around an unlabelled stratigraphy teaching block beside a bone replica and a plain stone flake, all visually distinct and stationary.

087|And even if a particular mark is genuinely from a tool, the next question remains open. How did the people obtain the animal they were processing?|Long-lens wide view of mature adult antelope grazing calmly in an open generic African landscape; slow lateral glide, no humans, predators or hunting action.
088|Our original groove has survived the first question only if the evidence supports it. Now we must resist the temptation to make it answer a second question too.|REUSE:001

089|First, we need to separate cause from sequence. Identifying a tooth mark tells us about contact. Establishing whether that contact came before or after another event takes additional evidence.|A modern optical microscope sits beside two clean synthetic coupons with deliberately intersecting artificial grooves; close side dolly, display turned away.

090|Where two well-preserved marks cross, their relationship may help establish a local order. But an apparent overlap in one photograph may be insufficient to resolve that order.|Extreme macro slow orbit around an enlarged resin cross-groove teaching model; clearly manufactured geometry, no authentic specimen claim or colour-coded data.

091|Surface loss can blur an intersection. An earlier event can disappear. And a clear local sequence on one specimen need not describe every bone at the site.|A mature researcher tilts a partially smoothed synthetic intersection model beneath a fixed raking light; close focus pull, modern laboratory.

092|Imagine that people processed one part of an animal, while a carnivore reached another part later. That possibility differs from a single animal being modified in one continuous event.|Two distinct clean adult-animal bone replicas lie in separate trays divided by a wide blank gap; slow overhead lateral glide, no live feeding or historical reenactment.

093|Now imagine several visits to the same place over a long interval. Bones from separate encounters could eventually enter the same deposit, complicating any simple sequence.|A transparent sediment teaching box contains animal-bone replicas at separate depths, with a thin visible sand layer between them; low slow side slide, no arrows.

094|Weathering and burial can preserve some surfaces while destroying others. The material available to us is therefore a filtered record, not a complete list of past actions.|Close overhead movement across a modern teaching collection of intact and deliberately smoothed animal-bone replicas in separate recesses; neutral laboratory lighting.

095|A collection also depends on recovery. Tiny fragments and heavily altered pieces can matter, even when they are less attractive than the best-preserved specimen in a display.|A clearly mature archaeologist gently passes dry sediment through a small sieve in a generic modern training excavation; slow medium side dolly, no discovery or text.

096|If only striking pieces are retained, the apparent pattern can change. A reference collection cannot repair information that was never recorded or material that was never recovered.|A mature researcher opens a plain museum drawer containing both large and small clean animal-bone teaching casts in separate compartments; overhead descent.

097|This is why documentation begins before the microscope. Where was the specimen found? What surrounded it? Which surfaces survived? What happened during excavation and conservation?|A mature field archaeologist photographs a neutral sediment section with a camera held level; medium lateral track, no rulers, notebooks, labels, numbers or visible screen.

098|The answers help distinguish an ancient modification from later damage, and a meaningful association from an accidental proximity. They give the close-up a history it cannot supply alone.|A gloved mature conservator examines an already separated resin fragment beside its fitted foam support, without scraping or cleaning it; close side push.

099|Our investigation has now widened from one groove to an entire chain of events. Only then can we ask what those events suggest about obtaining food.|Slow wide dolly from a specimen bench toward a reference room filled with plain closed drawers; contemporary laboratory, no people or readable content.

100|A genuine processing mark can support the conclusion that people handled an animal resource. It does not automatically tell us that they killed the animal themselves.|A plain stone flake rests beside a clean adult-animal bone replica on a modern research table; low close lateral glide, no contact, tissue or blood.

101|People could reach animals through different opportunities. A meal obtained after another predator's activity and a meal obtained through hunting may both leave traces of later processing.|An adult lion rests beneath a distant tree while adult antelope graze far away in a separate area; slow wide long-lens pan, no stalking, contact or remains.

102|The important questions include which resources remained, which anatomical parts were accessed, and how people and carnivores interacted with them. These are questions about patterns, not cinematic instincts.|A mature anatomist arranges clean resin replicas of distinct adult-animal limb elements into separate foam compartments; overhead orbit, no human bones or labels.

103|Researchers have built experimental models to compare combinations of cut, tooth, and percussion marks. Such models can help explore the order in which agents accessed animal resources.|A modern reference table holds three separate sets of cream artificial marked coupons in plain black trays; slow overhead descent, no graphs or dataset counts.

104|In a two thousand twelve study, Michael Pante and colleagues applied such models to Olduvai material, interpreting certain patterns as consistent with access after carnivores had removed flesh.|Slow aerial glide above a generic East African gorge with alternating sediment beds and a distant dry valley; no survey plans or reconstruction of a named excavation.

105|Other work has supported earlier access to substantial flesh. A two thousand twenty-one study used anatomical distributions of cut marks from several Olduvai assemblages to argue against frequent secondary access.|Mature contemporary researchers examine separate adult-animal skeletal teaching casts at three laboratory stations; medium lateral tracking, no visible datasets or written conclusions.

106|These approaches examine different patterns under particular assumptions. They show why the debate cannot be resolved by enlarging one attractive groove and placing a spear beside it.|An unlabelled wooden spear replica remains out of focus far behind a clean synthetic groove coupon on a modern teaching bench; close focus pull onto the coupon.

107|Early access to flesh and proof of a particular killing method are not interchangeable claims. The evidence for each needs to be considered at the appropriate scale.|Wide view of adult antelope walking calmly across open grassland, all clearly mature, no people or predators; smooth distant lateral glide.

108|This does not make hunting unknowable. It means the strongest argument should bring together relevant observations, rather than asking a tool mark to stand in for a missing event.|A mature archaeological researcher compares a bone cast with a separate inert wooden projectile teaching replica, both in closed-sided display trays; medium side dolly, no weapon use.

109|A prehistoric landscape held many opportunities and many competitors. Reducing every encounter to either a heroic hunt or a desperate leftover meal can hide that complexity.|Slow aerial glide across a generic savanna-river mosaic with adult herbivores visible at a great distance; no hunt, settlement or map overlay.
110|Our three questions still matter: who modified the bone, in what sequence, and how was the animal obtained? A good explanation keeps their answers separate until evidence connects them.|REUSE:005

111|Could better technology solve the problem? Modern three-dimensional microscopy can record surface shape and cross sections that a single flat photograph may not represent adequately.|A contemporary optical surface microscope moves across a clean resin specimen on its motorised stage; close low lateral tracking, screen facing away.

112|Researchers can compare depth, width, and other aspects of geometry. This creates more explicit observations, but a detailed measurement still needs a well-designed comparison to become an interpretation.|A large unlabelled physical model of a groove profile sits beside a modern optical microscope; slow close orbit, no computer readout or invented numerical values.

113|A precise scan of an ambiguous mark remains a precise record of an ambiguous mark. Resolution cannot, by itself, supply the missing agent or the lost context.|Macro push toward a synthetic worn groove under a microscope objective; realistic texture, no animated particles, inferred tool path or false diagnostic colours.

114|Experimental reference material is therefore essential. When the process that produced a sample is known, researchers can test how reliably other observers identify its traces.|A mature technician places a prepared synthetic coupon into a plain covered specimen holder while another mature researcher waits at a separate bench; medium side dolly.

115|Blind comparisons reduce the temptation to see what we expect. The observer examines the trace without being told which process produced it, then the result can be checked.|A mature researcher opens a plain covered specimen tray at an otherwise clear laboratory desk; close overhead descent, no identifiable codes or writing.

116|A study published in nineteen ninety-six tested distinctions among experimentally produced marks under controlled conditions. Its value lies in testing identification, rather than merely trusting a confident eye.|Two mature researchers independently inspect separate teaching coupons through ordinary magnifiers at matching desks; slow medium lateral track, no scoreboards or supposed historic footage.

117|Success with one reference collection does not make every archaeological surface equally easy to classify. Preservation, sampling, and unfamiliar processes can change the practical problem.|Macro focus pull between a smooth experimental coupon and a worn animal-bone teaching cast in separate holders; contemporary lab, physically distinct objects.

118|Computer classification introduces the same need for care. Researchers debate how well high-performing models generalise beyond the images and samples used to develop and evaluate them.|An adult computational researcher works at a contemporary laboratory computer with the display facing away; slow medium push toward a real microscope beside the workstation.

119|A responsible test asks about genuinely independent material, relevant alternatives, and error. A confident output is useful only when we understand the task it was actually tested on.|A mature researcher places a plain sealed specimen box on a different clear bench from the reference trays; slow side tracking, no lettering or verdict graphics.

120|Technology can strengthen the investigation by making observations more repeatable and comparisons more explicit. It should not become another impressive-looking substitute for the evidence we still need.|Slow overhead orbit around a modern microscope, resin groove model, and neutral sediment sample arranged with clear spacing on a laboratory bench.

121|Let us put those lessons together with a small thought experiment. Three trays, three different situations, and three chances to tell a story that goes too far.|A mature instructor places three plain dark trays in a row on a contemporary teaching table, each containing one clean synthetic animal-bone sample; slow overhead descent.

122|In the first tray, a worn specimen carries an isolated line. Its original location is uncertain. We can describe the mark, but the uncertainty must travel with it.|Close overhead slide across the first plain tray holding a deliberately worn synthetic animal-bone coupon with one shallow groove; modern demonstration, no codes or labels.

123|A dramatic reconstruction of a hunter would add information we do not possess.
